articles.title: In 2020, a metal detectorist found 933 Iron Age gold coins in an Essex field; another was found later, and the hoard is now on display
articles.summary: UK News: In 2020, a metal detectorist discovered 933 gold Iron Age coins on private land in Great Baddow, Essex, without permission to be detected there. Accor.
articles.body: In 2020, a metal detectorist discovered 933 gold Iron Age coins on private land in Great Baddow, Essex, without permission to be detected there. According to the official data available on Museum of Chelmsford’s site, the hoard, now known as the Great Baddow Hoard, is the largest recorded find of Iron Age gold coins ever made in Britain. Acquired by the Museum of Chelmsford in 2025 through a National Lottery Heritage Fund grant, it is thought to be linked to Julius Caesar's invasion of Britain. Here's how the find came about, what happened afterwards, and how it's being shared with the public.How a metal detectorist found 933 Iron Age gold coins in an Essex field in 2020The hoard was found on private land in Great Baddow by a metal detectorist who did not have permission to be detecting there. On discovering it, the finder initially failed to declare the find under the Treasure Act 1996, which limited how well the archaeological context could later be understood. According to Essex Heritage Trust, the hoard itself consists of 933 gold coins, 930 of which are Eastern British staters of the 'Whaddon Chase' type, produced in the North Thames region around 60 to 20 BC. The remaining three coins are a quarter stater, a Continental Gallo-Belgic E uniface stater, and an East Anglian 'Norfolk Wolf' stater, alongside fragments of what may have been a container or vessel.How few more coins were found at the Great Baddow hoard site laterBecause the coins were excavated in an uncontrolled way by the finder, and the accompanying artefacts were fragmentary, the archaeological context of the hoard was diminished. Shortly after the find was declared, the findspot was revisited by the Finds Liaison Officer for Essex, accompanied by a group of local experts. During this follow-up search, they recovered one further coin, though no additional surviving archaeological evidence was found at the site.The Great Baddow hoard may be linked to Julius CaesarThe hoard was found in territory traditionally associated with the Trinovantes, yet most of the coins are believed to have been produced in the region later linked to the Catuvellauni, suggesting a movement of that tribe eastwards. Some experts have suggested that the large number of gold staters being produced in eastern Britain at this time could be connected to Julius Caesar's invasion in 54BC, theorising the coins may have been intended as a tribute payment to the Roman general. While aggression between the Catuvellauni and Trinovantes is recorded in Roman sources, the hoard offers rare archaeological evidence to support it.How the hoard was acquired and where is it on display nowThe Great Baddow Hoard was acquired by the Museum of Chelmsford in May 2025, thanks to £250,000 in funding from the National Lottery Heritage Fund, alongside contributions from Chelmsford City Council, Friends of Chelmsford Museums, Essex Society for Archaeology and History, Essex Heritage Trust, Council for British Archaeology East, and Essex Numismatics Society.It is now recognised as the largest recorded hoard of Iron Age gold coins ever found in Britain. The hoard was on public display for the first time in a dedicated temporary exhibition, Timeless Treasures, in summer 2026, and will now be moving to permanent display at the museum from spring 2027.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Michelle Bachelet exits UN chief race after low poll support
articles.summary: Former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet ends her bid to be the first woman to lead the United Nations.
articles.body:
Former Chilean President Michelle Bachelet has withdrawn from the race to become the next United Nations secretary-general, ending her bid to become the first woman to lead the world body in its 80-year history.

Bachelet, 74, announced her decision on Saturday in a video posted on Instagram. “Today I announced that I have decided not to continue with my candidacy for the position of Secretary-General of the United Nations,” she said.

She added that she did not regret “having taken on this great challenge” even if “the time was not right” for the kind of candidacy she had sought to represent.

Her withdrawal comes after the UN Security Council released the third informal straw poll, held on Friday, in which she received just one “encourage” vote, 11 “discourage” votes and three “no opinion” votes, compared with six encouraging votes in July and two in August.

The same poll put Costa Rica’s Rebeca Grynspan, currently head of the UN’s Trade and Development body, in the lead with nine encouraging votes, closely followed by Guyana’s Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett with eight.

Other candidates still in the running include the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Rafael Grossi, former Senegalese President Macky Sall and Ecuadorian diplomat Maria Fernanda Espinosa.

To be recommended by the Security Council, a candidate needs at least nine of its 15 members to vote in favour and must avoid a veto from any of the five permanent members – China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States – before a final vote in the General Assembly.

Bachelet was nominated by Chile in February with backing from Brazil and Mexico. Only one Latin American, Peru’s Javier Perez de Cuellar, has ever held the UN’s top job, and an unofficial rotation among regions had put Latin America in line for this cycle.

Whoever succeeds Antonio Guterres, the current secretary-general, whose term ends on December 31, will take charge of an organisation grappling with dynamic crises.

Guterres warned member states earlier this year that the UN faced “imminent financial collapse”, with $1.57bn in unpaid dues piled up by the end of 2025 and only a fraction of countries fully paid up.

World leaders converge on New York next week for the General Assembly’s annual high-level session, opening Tuesday under the theme “Restoring Trust, Managing Transformation”.

Guterres warned that geopolitical divides among major powers – some of whom “themselves violate international law and sit in the Security Council” – have left the body deadlocked on Gaza , Ukraine and other crises, a dysfunction the still-unresolved race to succeed him will do little to fix on its own.

articles.title: ‘Sell your wife’: Delhi's killer couple who murdered executive Yuvraj Singh Manchanda under scanner for frauds worth crores

articles.body: NEW DELHI: “Sell your wife/do anything, just repay this,” read a WhatsApp message cited in an FIR filed by a senior executive who allegedly lost over Rs 1.2 crore in a fraud racket involving Yuvraj Singh Manchanda’s former colleague Anya Vats and her partner Sanyam Sachdeva. Police are now probing whether Manchanda, who was allegedly killed by the couple in Gurgaon on Sept 6, had learnt about their alleged activities.Fake ED notice allegedly used to trap schoolmatePolice have found that the couple allegedly targeted people close to them, including a former schoolmate of Sachdeva, who was duped of over Rs 1.2 crore after receiving a fake Enforcement Directorate notice. The cheating case was registered at Parliament Street police station this August.The complainant, a senior vice-president at a non-banking financial company that is a subsidiary of a public sector bank, told police that the extortion began in Sept 2024, when he received the fraudulent notice on WhatsApp allegedly involving an acquaintance.According to the complainant, Sachdeva, a former schoolmate, along with Vats, allegedly claimed to have high-level government connections and offered to settle the matter.The duo allegedly also used fabricated notices in the name of the Union home ministry, citing fake cases under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act and Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, to coerce him into transferring money.Rs 1.2 crore transferred, then another Rs 26 crore demandedThe complainant allegedly transferred over Rs 1.2 crore primarily to Vats’ bank account, using his personal savings, loans and family borrowings.Vats later allegedly demanded another Rs 26 crore, claiming that Rs 13.8 crore had been paid to government agencies on his behalf. The complainant eventually realised that he had allegedly fallen prey to a fraud racket and approached police.In the FIR, the complainant also mentioned the WhatsApp message threatening him to repay the money before Diwali.Property case involving Sachdeva’s estranged wifeSources said Sachdeva had also allegedly duped his estranged wife over a property worth around Rs 4.5 crore in Greater Noida. A third case involved a domestic violence complaint filed by the wife.Police are now examining whether Manchanda had learnt about any of these alleged activities.The inquiry also revealed that Vats and Sachdeva had called Manchanda on the pretext of a client meeting on the day of the murder.A family friend of Manchanda said, “Yuvraj had informed his fiance that he was meeting the clients with Vats in 20 minutes and would call back soon.”Phones being examined for body disposal searchesInvestigators have seized an illegal pistol and the victim’s car, and both are being examined by forensic teams.Electronic equipment, including the accused’s phones, has been sent to the Forensic Science Laboratory to determine whether the couple had searched online for ways to dispose of a body.Cops have also found that the accused stopped in Vrindavan, Uttar Pradesh, while fleeing to Uttarakhand after the murder. They suspect this might have been part of an attempt to dodge police.‘Continuously changing statements’ on money dispute“They have been continuously changing their statements about the alleged monetary dispute with Manchanda,” sources said.“Vats claimed that the victim had threatened her, but no evidence has been found so far,” an officer said.Family raises issue over ZIPNET entryManchanda’s family has claimed that even on Sept 16, Gurgaon Police uploaded his entry in the “Unidentified persons found” portal on ZIPNET instead of “Unidentified dead bodies”. The body was found in Gurgaon on Sept 10.Gurgaon Police, however, said there was no delay on its part and Delhi Police should have lodged a missing FIR within 24 hours of receiving the information from the family.They should also have flagged it to Gurgaon Police timely, knowing that Manchanda worked in Gurgaon, said a senior officer.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.summary: US News: US President Donald Trump on Saturday criticised the United States Supreme Court over its rulings on tariffs and birthright citizenship, accusing the .
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Saturday criticised the United States Supreme Court over its rulings on tariffs and birthright citizenship, accusing the top court of lacking the courage to “make America great again”.In a post on Truth Social, Trump described the court's decisions as “faulty, political and ridiculous”, claiming they had cost the country trillions of dollars and “forever damaged” the process through which people become US citizens.“Unfortunately, the United States Supreme Court has lacked the courage to make America great again,” Trump said.“Over the last 6 months, with their faulty, political, and ridiculous decisions on tariffs and birthright citizenship, they have cost the United States of America trillions of Dollars, and forever damaged the way people become citizens of our great Country. It has been a sad chapter in the life and times of America, but we will prevail!” he added.Trump's remarks come amid a series of legal battles between his administration and the Supreme Court over his tariff policies and efforts to restrict birthright citizenship.In February, the Supreme Court struck down most of Trump's sweeping tariff measures, ruling that the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not authorise the president to impose the extensive import duties.The ruling triggered a major refund process for importers that had paid the disputed tariffs. According to a US Customs and Border Protection court filing, around USD 100 billion in refunds had been completed and sent to the US Treasury for disbursement by July 31. About USD 128.68 billion in potential and certified refunds had been accepted for processing.The tariff ruling also created financial and administrative challenges for the US government, with customs authorities developing a new system to calculate and process refunds for affected importers.Trump has continued to defend his tariff strategy, arguing that the measures are aimed at protecting American industries, boosting domestic manufacturing and addressing trade imbalances.His administration has also faced legal challenges over its attempt to restrict birthright citizenship. The administration has argued that existing interpretations of the 14th Amendment permit citizenship restrictions in certain circumstances, while opponents have challenged the policy in court.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: Deepanshu Shokeen’s victory as an Independent has emerged as the most striking story of this year’s Delhi University Students’ Union (DUSU) election not just because he won the vice president’s post by a huge margin, but because he did so after breaking away from Congress affiliated NSUI, the organisation with which he had been associated for long.The 21 year old postgraduate student of Buddhist studies is the son of a DTC bus conductor and an anganwadi worker.A former member of National Students’ Union of India, Shokeen, a resident of Peeragarhi, fought the election as an Independent following a dispute over ticket distribution.At 30,615, Shokeen secured the highest number of votes among all central panel candidates and won by 13,705 votes.Analysts said his strong support base among Jat students, and beyond the community, helped him build a distinct identity outside the established ABVP NSUI contest.His high visibility campaign, including his decision to remain barefoot while seeking justice for students killed in the Satya Niketan building collapse, further strengthened that independent identity.Sidestepping questions on the split, Shokeen said, “Irrespective of who I represent, I am going to focus on students’ issues. The major focus should be on who can address students’ issues and whom students believe in, not which party or community they come from.”NSUI’s vice presidential candidate, Vir Chatrath, claimed Shokeen was not denied a ticket and was offered the presidential post.In the presidential contest, at the end of 10 rounds, NSUI’s Vijay Shankar Meena led ABVP’s Yash Dabas by 524 votes, 11,966 to 11,442. But Dabas eventually won by 2,053 votes.Independent candidate Samarth Beniwal, who was also associated with NSUI, polled 819 votes. In the joint secretary race, the contest went beyond the traditional two party fight.At the end of 10 rounds, Samajwadi Chhatra Sabha candidate Vishesh Yadav was leading with 8,501 votes, ahead of NSUI’s Gopal Choudhary at 8,135 and ABVP’s Lakshay Raj Singh at 8,125.The race subsequently shifted, with Lakshay winning with 16,615 votes, just 837 ahead of Yadav’s tally of 15,778. The NSUI candidate polled 15,206 votes.The results point to a DUSU contest that remained dominated by ABVP in terms of seats, but was not a sweep and was considerably less straightforward in terms of votes.The outcome shows a growing space for candidates and outfits operating outside that ABVP NSUI binary.An NSUI rebel’s lead remained substantial throughout the race for the VP’s post, an SCS candidate came within 837 votes of taking the joint secretary’s post, while the presidential race stayed within a few hundred votes through the middle of counting before ABVP finally pulled away.The results also raise questions about the Left alliance’s ability to convert its political mobilisation into votes.Compared with 2025, the AISA SFI alliance’s performance was virtually unchanged in the presidential race, with Ananya Raturi polling 5,377 votes against 5,385 last year, but its tally fell in the other three contests, from 4,163 to 2,383 for vice president, 9,535 to 8,734 for secretary, articles.title: Australia seeks big tech support for internet safety, AI regulation
articles.summary: PM Anthony Albanese asks Apple boss Tim Cook to back Canberra’s online safety laws to ‘keep Australians safe’.
articles.body:
The Australian government is seeking support from global tech giants as it works to strengthen the country’s online safety laws and artificial intelligence (AI) regulations.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, who met Apple’s executive chairman Tim Cook at the tech company’s headquarters in Cupertino, California, on Saturday, said that “Australia can’t do it alone” when it came to protecting children from the dangers of the internet.

“We spoke about what we’re doing to protect children from online harm and the work ahead,” Albanese wrote on social media.

“We’re putting stronger rules in place to keep Australians safe online,” he said. “And now, big tech companies like Apple are stepping up too.”

Albanese, who is also in the United States for the United Nations General Assembly, used his trip to call for stronger AI regulation after dire safety warnings from industry leaders.

Australia will introduce new standards for AI by the end of the year, he said.

In a video posted to his X account, Albanese said his Labor government is “making sure technology works for Australians”, and not the other way around.

In a post on X, Cook also said he shared with Albanese new “strong and intuitive controls to help keep kids safe online”.

New Australian legislation unveiled this month would place a “duty of care” requirement on the firms behind popular platforms, such as Facebook, TikTok and Instagram, and allow users to turn off their algorithms.

The draft laws will be introduced to parliament later this year after consultation with social media companies, industry bodies and civil society groups.

The opposition Liberal-National Coalition opposes the bill “in its current form”, according to a statement published on September 10, saying that it “contains inadequate safeguards for free speech and journalism, and leaves too much power in the hands of the Communications Minister”.

Australia implemented legislation barring children under 16 from social media platforms last year as part of a world-first crackdown designed to protect children from online bullying and “predatory algorithms”.

However, data last month found that Australians under 16 continued using social media apps such as Instagram and TikTok despite the ban.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran calls Gaza situation ‘unjustifiable’ after Palestine controversy
articles.summary: The British singer addresses fans at his concert in Philadelphia as his US Loop Tour resumes.
articles.body:
British pop star Ed Sheeran has made his first comments on the controversy that plunged his North America Loop Tour into turmoil, saying that the situation in Gaza is “catastrophic”, “unjustifiable” and “disproportionate”.

Sheeran made the remarks as he opened his show at the Lincoln Financial Field stadium in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, where his tour resumed on Saturday night.

The pop singer has faced a wave of criticism after his opening act, American rapper Macklemore, was dropped from the lineup over his pro-Palestine comments at a concert in New Jersey earlier this month.

Macklemore’s comments drew backlash from owners of stadiums hosting Sheeran’s future tour dates. Sheeran has denied being behind the decision, blaming the tour promoter.

According to US media reports, the start time for the concert was pushed back two and a half hours because there were no opening acts and Sheeran performed solo.

All of Sheeran’s four supporting acts , including American singer Billie Eilish’s brother and musical collaborator, Finneas, walked out on Sheeran, issuing public statements citing their support for Palestinians.

Finneas and his sister have been outspoken about their support for Palestine before.

“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” he said on Instagram last Tuesday, adding: “I stand with Palestine and its people.”

A group of about 50 pro-Palestinian demonstrators rallied outside the stadium before the show on Saturday, waving Palestinian flags and chanting “Free, free Palestine.”

Hillary Steinberg, 34, of Philadelphia, said she got tickets a year ago but got a refund and attended the demonstration instead, disappointed that Sheeran did not take a stand.

“I was, until this week, a big Ed Sheeran fan,” Steinberg told the Associated Press news agency. “I think all art is political, and all music is political, and so this choice, even though he was saying that he wasn’t complicit, is a political choice.”

The controversy did not matter to concertgoers who spoke to the Reuters news agency on Saturday before Sheeran took to the stage.

Joy VanRuler, 55, of Pottstown, Pennsylvania, said she supports both Sheeran and Macklemore.

“It doesn’t need to be political,” VanRuler said. “It’s about the music, and we support both of them and it’s all good.”

articles.body: Smoke rose near King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh after Yemen's Houthi rebels launched a large-scale attack on Saudi Arabia on Saturday. Two explosions were heard in the capital, while some flights were delayed.The Houthis said they targeted "sensitive targets" in Riyadh and a Saudi Aramco facility in Yanbu. The group said it used ballistic and cruise missiles and drones in the attacks.Saudi air defences later said they had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile targeting Riyadh.Smoke seen near airportVideos showed a plume of smoke rising near King Khalid International Airport after the second explosion.Saudi authorities had earlier issued an aerial threat alert for Riyadh. They later announced that the danger had passed. The alert was reportedly the first such warning issued for the Saudi capital since tensions with the Houthis escalated.The Houthis reportedly targeted the fuel storage infrastructure at the airport triggering large plumes of smoke to rise up.There were no immediate reports of casualties or major damage in Riyadh.Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said the group had launched two major operations.The first targeted what he called "sensitive targets" in Riyadh. The second targeted a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco in Yanbu, a major industrial and energy hub on the Red Sea coast."The two operations were successful," Sarea said.He claimed that large fires broke out at the targeted sites. The claims could not be independently verified.Saudi Arabia says attacks were thwartedThe Saudi-led coalition said its air defences intercepted the missile targeting Riyadh. It also said attacks on Baish, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu had been thwarted.Coalition spokesperson Turki Al-Maliki said the attacks targeted "civilians and civilian objects". He also warned that Saudi Arabia would take "appropriate measures" to deter further attacks.The Houthis denied deliberately targeting civilians.Sarea said the attacks were in response to increased Saudi airstrikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen. He vowed to continue what he called an "escalation for escalation" strategy until Saudi airstrikes stop and restrictions on Yemen are lifted.The latest attack marks a major escalation in the confrontation between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia.The current round of fighting began in mid-July after strikes on Houthi-controlled Sanaa International Airport. The strikes came as an Iranian passenger plane carrying a senior Houthi delegation was returning from Iran.The Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of being behind the strikes. They then launched missile and drone attacks in retaliation.On July 20, the group announced a ban on Saudi shipping through the Bab el-Mandab Strait. It has since claimed several attacks on Saudi tankers and oil facilities.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Morocco’s PJD: what has the party learned from its dramatic fall
articles.summary: After its 2021 defeat, the party with an Islamic reference is rebuilding under Abdelilah Benkirane. Can it regain trust?
articles.body:
Morocco’s Justice and Development Party (PJD) went from a decade of being the main political beneficiary of the country’s post-2011 reforms to suffering a dramatic electoral defeat in 2021.

The party won 107 of the 395 seats in Parliament in the November 2011 election, after protests that year called for political reform, greater accountability and a more responsive government. Its leader, Abdelilah Benkirane, became head of government.

Morocco’s 2011 constitutional changes expanded the formal powers of Parliament and government while retaining significant authority for the monarchy. The king appoints the head of government from the party that comes first in the House of Representatives, while he chairs the Council of Ministers, where strategic orientations of state policy are considered.

In the 2016 election, the PJD increased its seats to 125, but Benkirane spent months unable to form a governing coalition. In March 2017, King Mohammed VI ended his mandate and appointed Saadeddine Othmani to replace him. The PJD remained in government until its electoral collapse four years later.

In the September 2021 election, the party fell from 125 seats to just 13, losing 112. The National Rally of Independents (RNI) won 102 seats and became the largest party.

How much of the comeback rests on Benkirane?

Benkirane’s return raises another question: How much of the PJD’s comeback is being built around him?

A recent Al Jazeera Studies analysis describes Benkirane as a political “brand” whose long public career, media presence and direct communication style have created a personal profile that can function as electoral capital for the party.

It examines whether his visibility and personal appeal can help the PJD rebuild after its 2021 collapse.

Benkirane remains one of Morocco’s most recognisable political figures. But his return does not by itself show that the PJD has rebuilt its support.

The party lost 112 seats in 2021; its task now is to turn the attention generated by its leader into support for the party itself.

The PJD’s 2026 programme contains 467 measures across five broad areas: identity and family; political and institutional reform; public services and social protection; the economy and employment; and foreign policy.

It calls for greater transparency in public procurement, rules addressing conflicts of interest and illicit enrichment, and improvements to public services. It also highlights housing, social protection, food, water and energy sovereignty.

Its programme foregrounds practical issues such as prices, jobs, schools, hospitals and corruption.

Saad al-Sabahi, 38, who works with the PJD’s regional secretariat in Casablanca-Settat, said the programme was developed through studies, consultation meetings and proposals submitted through an online platform.

“These commitments cover a range of sectors and areas affecting the lives of the Moroccan people,” he told Al Jazeera, pointing to political participation, fighting corruption, public education, healthcare, employment and economic sovereignty.

“These commitments, among others, form the basis of the agreement between the party and voters. We will work to fulfil and implement them with integrity and competence,” al-Sabahi said.

The PJD says one of its main lessons from the 2021 defeat has been the need to reorganise internally and examine more critically its years in government.

“The party was able to overcome its crisis following its extraordinary and regular congresses, and after Secretary-General Abdelilah Benkirane took over the leadership,” al-Sabahi said. “The party also reorganised its internal affairs through communication and the renewal of its structures.”

The party’s own assessment of the 2021 defeat includes criticism of its political and organisational choices. It has also accused unnamed actors of undermining democratic choice and pointed to what it describes as electoral corruption and disinformation.

Those are the PJD’s explanations for the result, rather than independently established findings. But the scale of its losses forced the party to confront how far its record in government had separated it from parts of its former support base.

That matters particularly when it comes to younger voters.

Imane Traifi, 37, of the PJD Youth, said the party needed to create sustained opportunities for young people to take part in political life rather than treating them simply as voters during election campaigns.

“We are keen to ensure that young people move from being recipients to becoming participants, initiators and people who take on responsibility,” she told Al Jazeera.

However, a question for any future PJD government is not only what it would seek to change, but what it could change once in office.

Benkirane repeatedly referred to “ghosts and crocodiles” as a metaphor for powerful or hidden interests that he said had obstructed his government when it was in power.

The clearest example is the party’s position on Israel.

The PJD has campaigned against Morocco’s normalisation with Israel and continues to support the Palestinian cause. Its 2026 programme explicitly calls for opposition to normalisation. Yet Morocco restored diplomatic ties with Israel in 2020 while the PJD was in government and Saadeddine Othmani was head of government.

The PJD opposed the move, while Othmani later defended it as a state decision and said Morocco’s support for the Palestinian cause remained unchanged. The agreement went ahead in December 2020 as part of a US-brokered deal that included Washington’s recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara.

Six years later, the relationship has moved further. On September 16, Morocco and Israel agreed to elevate their diplomatic missions to embassy level and appoint ambassadors, while also expanding air travel and advancing economic and trade agreements.

The PJD reaffirmed its opposition to normalisation and cooperation with Israel the following day, describing its position as longstanding.

But it also leaves a question for the party’s return: If such forces were powerful enough to constrain the government then, what has changed?

Has the PJD developed a different understanding of the limits of government authority or will it find itself once again beset by “ghosts and crocodiles”?

The PJD has made clear on several occasions that the change it seeks is from within Morocco’s existing political and constitutional system, rather than a challenge to the monarchy itself.

Benkirane has repeatedly reaffirmed his support for the monarchy while arguing that elected institutions should play their role in governing and improving the country.

That distinction is important to understanding the PJD’s return. Its opposition to policies such as normalisation with Israel sits alongside its acceptance of a constitutional and political framework in which the monarchy retains a central role in strategic state decisions.

Under the constitution, the king chairs the Council of Ministers, which considers the strategic orientations of state policy.

That applies not only to Israel but to other areas where major policy decisions remain closely tied to the monarchy.

For the PJD, rebuilding means more than recovering the seats it lost in 2021. It means showing what it learned from a decade in government, what it can deliver and how it would avoid the political costs of its collapse.

Al-Sabahi said the party wanted to regain what he described as the gains citizens had previously enjoyed.

“We will work to restore the gains that citizens previously enjoyed and to restore their dignity and rights,” he told Al Jazeera.

Yassine Elachiri, a member of the National Bureau of PJD Youth and the party’s National Council, said the relationship with younger Moroccans had to be built over time rather than during campaigns.

“Earning the trust of a new generation of young people cannot be reduced to electoral mobilisation or short-term campaigns in the run-up to voting day,” he said. “Rather, it is a cumulative process built on sustained engagement, guidance, training and creating opportunities for young people to participate actively in public affairs.”

“Our goal is not simply to reach young people at the moment of an election, but to build a lasting relationship with them based on trust, training and active participation,” Elachiri said.

articles.title: US military strikes alleged narco-trafficking vessel in Caribbean, killing 4 'narco-terrorists'
articles.summary: Video shows a Caribbean vessel erupting into a fireball as SOUTHCOM says it killed four alleged narco-terrorists in a drug trafficking strike.
articles.body: The U.S. military on Saturday carried out a lethal strike on a vessel in the Caribbean that it said was involved in drug trafficking, killing four alleged "narco-terrorists," according to U.S. Southern Command (SOUTHCOM). "On September 19, under the direction of #SOUTHCOM, Joint Task Force Western Hemisphere executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Caribbean," SOUTHCOM said in a statement. "Confirmed intelligence revealed the vessel's active involvement in narco-trafficking," the statement continued. SOUTHCOM said four alleged "narco-terrorists" were killed during the operation. NEWLY UNCLASSIFIED PENTAGON IMAGES SHOW SUSPECTED DRUG BOATS AS OFFICIAL ISSUES DEADLY WARNING Saturday's strike comes amid a monthslong campaign launched by the Trump administration aimed at dismantling cartel-linked trafficking networks. SOUTHCOM has conducted dozens of strikes in the Eastern Pacific and Caribbean targeting vessels it says are connected to "narco-terrorists." On Sept. 9, the military said it carried out a strike on a vessel involved in narco-trafficking that resulted in three deaths. US FORCES OBLITERATE SUSPECTED 'NARCO-TERRORIST' VESSEL IN LETHAL EASTERN PACIFIC STRIKE, KILLING 3 Following Saturday's strike, the Trump administration's campaign targeting suspected cartel vessels has resulted in at least 231 deaths tied to at least 69 reported strikes over roughly one year. Video of Saturday's operation released by SOUTHCOM shows a vessel moving through the water before erupting into a massive fireball. In recent weeks, SOUTHCOM has also released several videos showing military personnel intercepting and boarding vessels allegedly involved in narco-trafficking before removing their crews and sinking the boats. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Many of the operations recently highlighted by SOUTHCOM have targeted vessels allegedly tied to Los Choneros, which the military has described as a violent "narco-terrorist" organization.

articles.title: A young boy vanished in the desert one year ago. Why are there still no clues?
articles.summary: Little Gus Lamont was wearing a gray sun hat over his long blond curls and a blue Minions T-shirt as he played in the sand outside his grandparents’ house in the Australian outback last September.
articles.body: Little Gus Lamont was wearing a gray sun hat over his long blond curls and a blue Minions T-shirt as he played in the sand outside his grandparents’ house in the Australian outback last September. When his grandmother went to check on him, he was gone. The disappearance of the four-year-old boy from the fenced front yard of a home on a remote sheep station, almost 30 miles from the nearest town, sparked the largest police search in South Australian state history. Over hours then days, hundreds of police officers, military personnel and other search teams scoured a 3.4-mile radius around the house on foot. But there was no sign of Gus – not his hat, nor his shirt, nor the small boots he was wearing. Detectives drained three dams, searched six mineshafts and sent up drones with specialized cameras to take detailed imagery, later analyzed with artificial intelligence. Still, nothing. Then five months later, Police dropped a bombshell announcement –– the case was now considered a “major crime.” Young children go missing all the time, and statistics will tell you that most are found within hours, inside their own homes, or having wandered not much more than a mile away. Some are caught on doorbell or security cameras that offer vital clues; others are taken within sight of witnesses who can point police toward a potential abductor. None of that applies in the case of Gus Lamont. Police narrowed their focus to three family members who were at the property on September 27, 2025, when Gus disappeared: his mother and her parents. Detective Superintendent Darren Fielke, of South Australia Police, told reporters in February that “inconsistencies” had been found in information provided by the family members. “As a result of these inconsistencies and investigations into them, a person who resides at Oak Park Station… is no longer cooperating with us,” Fielke said. Fielke ruled out Gus’ parents as suspects, leaving the finger of suspicion pointing at one of his grandparents –– who has issued a public denial. Seven months on, no one has been charged and, publicly at least, police seem no closer to solving what’s become one of Australia’s most cryptic missing-person cases. Isolated outback station From the air, Oak Park Station is a dot on a vast, mostly barren landscape scattered with trees, low-lying vegetation and long lines of roads and fences, around 150 miles north of Adelaide. Two long dirt tracks lead miles away from the nearest town, Yunta, past other pastoral stations and through several gates that police say were regularly locked by landowners. Until last September, the residents largely kept to themselves – it wasn’t hard given the distance and the long hours needed to maintain a working sheep station. The ranch is owned by Gus’ grandparents, Josie and Shannon Murray, the parents of Gus’ mother Jessica Murray. Josie Murray and Jess had been mustering sheep in the paddock with their dogs and returned to the house at about 5:30 p.m. on the day Gus disappeared, Josie told CNN affiliate Channel 7’s Spotlight program. Shannon had been at the homestead looking after Gus and his little brother Ronnie and had taken her eyes off him while he amused himself, as he often did around the property. “Shan said that Gus was just down near what we called the bomb shelter, playing,” Josie said in June. “When we had a look, no sign. And we said to Shan, ‘When did you last see him? And she said, ‘5 o’clock.’ And so, in that … half-hour time frame, he disappeared.” Josie said Gus loved to explore the property on foot or on his bike, and had wandered away before, but never too far. Video released by the family to aid the search showed Gus in a large hat, using his bare feet to push his balance bike across a rocky driveway. “He loved his push bike, pushing that around and just letting it roll down the hill,” Josie recalled. “He was just a normal happy four-year-old child.” On day one, daylight was fading When they realized Gus was gone, his mother and grandparents started searching for him around the property, starting with the cellar they were constructing, the pool, and all the buildings. ‘We’ve got 45 minutes of daylight,” Josie remembered telling Jess, so they jumped on their motorbikes to check further afield: the tanks, the dam, the shearing shed. By 8 p.m., the roads around Oak Park Station were bathed in a darkness only broken by headlights and torches, and the family realized it was time to call the police. One officer from the nearest town arrived to help them search the property, while a police helicopter with an infrared camera circled above. Daybreak saw the start of a foot search that spread 36 square miles (94 square kilometers), as drones scanned the dusty land. But high-tech gear has limitations in such an unforgiving environment. Outback sand caught in scrubs and desert grass retained warmth long after the sun went down, meaning “every single bush looked like a heat target,” said Daniel Wood, CEO of Working Drones Australia. Daytime temperatures were close to 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), and the nights were cold, less than 10 degrees Celsius. “When it gets dark, most small kids have the ability to find somewhere to sleep, whether it be under a park bench or under a bush or something like that,” said retired Queensland Police Senior Sergeant Jim Whitehead, who wrote Australia’s search and rescue guidelines. “But they don’t have the skills to find water, to find food, to find heat, to modify their environment,” he added. And searching for children requires looking at the world from their point of view. “They generally never walk in a straight line. They’re often doing things that adults won’t understand; looking for dappled light, or following a butterfly, or even following a pet.” Was Gus abducted? When a child goes missing in the city, police are on alert for a possible abduction. In the US, roadblocks are erected as the FBI’s Child Abduction Rapid Response team swings into action. Drivers in the vicinity are questioned, neighboring households searched, and any available video scrutinized for suspects. In the sparsely populated Australian outback, help takes time to arrive. A second police officer called to the farmhouse that night got lost, and despite the family’s best instructions, gave up trying to find them, Josie Murray told 7 Spotlight. Oak Park Station is not signposted, and finding the property requires knowledge of the area, Fielke told reporters in February, as he explained why police didn’t believe Gus had been abducted. “It’s not a place that you just go to,” he said. No unexplained vehicle tracks were located running to or from the property, he said, and everyone in the area with a risk profile of child offending had been questioned and discounted. Gus had no routine that regularly put him outside his grandparents’ house at that time of day, so it was “very unlikely” that someone had compiled a dossier of his movements and was there at exactly the right time to snatch him, Fielke said. “The opportunity for anybody to abduct Gus is extremely low.” Josie Murray disagrees. She believes it’s entirely plausible that someone drove along the remote road and snatched Gus from outside their house. And she says that evidence of an intruder – tire tracks or footprints – could have been lost in the flurry of activity that whipped up dust on roads around the property in the early days of the search. “There would be something out here. There has to be something,” she told 7 Spotlight. A search by air and AI Hope of finding Gus alive faded as the days and weeks passed. And with no answers, the aerial search zone was widened to 706 square kilometers (273 square miles). If he died in the bush, his body should be out there. Or at the very least a scrap of clothing. In late October, police turned to Nearmap, a company that captures images for insurance claims, in far higher resolution than anything you’ll see on Google Earth. From a plane flying at 6,000 feet, their photos can show cracks in roof tiles after a hailstorm. Their plane flew for several days over the entire search zone, taking photos so large and detailed that they needed to be analyzed by AI. For that, Nearmap turned to Sci-eye, a company that uses its AI models to count kangaroos, to inform government culls. In the images of Oak Park Station, Sci-eye found 10,000 sheep, 6,000 goats, 6,000 red kangaroos, a few hundred emus, grey kangaroos, wallaroos, and a few wedge-tailed eagles. But they didn’t find Gus Lamont. Fifteen inconclusive items were flagged to police but “there weren’t any objects in there that were obviously related to what we would expect from Gus,” said Andrew Walsh, Sci-eye’s founding director. Police checked the inconclusive objects, and found nothing. The technology isn’t perfect, Walsh said; if Gus had crawled beneath a bush to sleep, the camera wouldn’t necessarily find him. “Maybe he wandered off and is hidden under a tree, and we can’t see under that specific tree,” he added. Was he taken by an animal? A friend of the family, Bill Harbison, shared a theory with 7 Spotlight that maybe a wedge-tailed eagle had swooped down and picked him up. Raptor expert Ian Falkenberg said it’s an example of the misleading folklore shared among farmers about the power of Australia’s largest bird of prey. “Could an eagle have taken the child and flown off into the distance? Absolutely not,” he told CNN. Female wedge-tailed eagles are larger than the males, but even they don’t weigh more than a few kilograms, he said. And both are too light to lift a child of Gus’ age – roughly 13 kilograms, according to pediatric guidelines. Falkenberg said wedge-tailed eagles have an undeserved reputation for killing livestock, and in all his years, he hasn’t come across any credible reports of attacks on humans. Dingoes are a different story. The native dogs are known to have killed baby Azaria Chamberlain, who was taken in the outback in 1980, and mauled Canadian tourist Piper James, who died on K’Gari off the coast of Queensland earlier this year. But according to Walsh from Sci-eye, no dingoes were seen in the massive search area around Oak Park Station. Highly venomous brown snakes are also found in the area, and a bite could have killed a small child. But even if Gus had sadly died in the outback, an influx of scavengers would likely have alerted searchers to the presence of his body, experts said. Birds would have been circling in the sky above, said Falkenberg. Feral pigs are also known for scavenging carcasses across most of Australia. But Walsh said Sci-eye’s analysis found no feral pigs in the search area. “Are they actually here?” The absence of clues, even a scrap of clothing, has pointed police in a direction initially considered unthinkable. “When we don’t find anything at all, then we’ve got to start thinking: Are they actually here?” said Whitehead, the search expert. “Were they missing in the first place?” SA Police didn’t name their suspect when they announced they were treating Gus’ disappearance as a “major crime,” but it wasn’t long before word spread that their suspect was Gus’ grandmother – Josie Murray. Police had earlier said they were considering three options: Gus had wandered off; he was abducted; or someone known to him was involved in his disappearance and suspected death. Having discounted the first two options, the possibility narrowed to the third. “They think that I buried him,” Josie told 7 Spotlight in her only public interview. “For so many reasons, it’s ludicrous,” she added. “To think that I could face up to the trauma of doing that would also be ridiculous.” When asked by CNN to confirm that Josie Murray was a suspect, SA Police declined to comment, citing the active investigation. Josie and Shannon Murray used to be married, before Josie transitioned in the 1990s. They remain business partners, living and working together at the property. Their friend, Bill Harbison, suggested to Spotlight that police had focused their attention on Josie because of her “transgender situation.” That was quickly rejected by South Australia’s Deputy Police Commissioner Linda Williams, who told 7 News the claim was “nonsense.” In January, detectives seized several items during a search of Oak Park Station, including a vehicle, a motorcycle, and some electronic devices. By May, police said forensic examination of those items produced no new lines of inquiry. Nor did they help exclude any suspect, they added. In June, Josie faced court on an unrelated charge after police found an unregistered silencer during a search of Oak Park Station. In Australia, silencers are classed as prohibited weapons, and owning one requires a permit. Her lawyer, Andrew Ey, told the court: “This isn’t some James Bond movie where you’ve had a villain or an assassin walking around the corners taking out targets with little more than a whisper of a gun – that is not what the court is dealing with.” Murray was fined around 10,000 Australian dollars ($7,000) and barred from holding a gun license for five years. Murray’s lawyer did not respond to CNN’s request for an interview. Lawyers acting for Shannon Murray told CNN she was cooperating with police and had no further comment. Falkenberg, the raptor expert, said he knew the Murrays for a decade or so when he worked near Oak Park Station, years before Gus was born. “Most of those pastoral people out there, they’re salt of the earth… That community, they help each other. They’re part of the community,” he said. “Sitting around the kitchen table talking to them… they were delightful people.” People are still looking for Gus, one year after he disappeared. Search parties were sent out again in May after heavy rain in the hope that water would uncover more clues, to no avail. Nearmap took more images of the search zone in August that Walsh from Sci-eye is still examining. “It looks very different from the first time the plane was out,” he said. Rain has brought new life to the barren, red earth and, rather than giving up new clues, it may have further concealed any evidence of Gus’ whereabouts. “If there’s anything obvious out there that we feel should be reported back, then we will immediately let the police know,” Walsh said. Whitehead, the police search expert, often testifies in the Coroner’s Court to comment on the strength of the police search when a person goes missing. Asked whether SA Police had done enough to find the young boy, he said: “Absolutely.” “They searched way beyond any chance that Gus could have survived by himself,” Whitehead said. Gus’ parents have kept a low profile throughout. After police announced they were treating his disappearance as a “major crime,” they thanked the search parties and urged anyone with information to come forward. “Even the smallest detail could give us the answers we so desperately need,” they said in a statement. “All we want is to bring Gus home and understand what happened to our beautiful boy.”

articles.title: Why Buckingham Palace’s bearskin caps might soon be a relic of the past
articles.summary: Soldiers in bright red uniforms and tall, black fur hats outside Buckingham Palace are a familiar sight for anyone who’s visited London.
articles.body: Soldiers in bright red uniforms and tall, black fur hats outside Buckingham Palace are a familiar sight for anyone who’s visited London. But the distinctive caps – among the most recognizable symbols of the British monarchy – have become increasingly contentious for their use of real bear fur. Now, a group of British lawmakers has called on the government to end the use of real bearskins in the ceremonial headpieces worn by the King’s Guard. The practice is “impossible to justify” and should be replaced with synthetic alternatives, according to cross-party members of parliament (MPs). In a letter to Defence Minister Luke Pollard this week, 18 MPs and one member of the House of Lords urged the government to stop using bear pelts sourced from legal culls in Canada and instead adopt faux-fur alternatives. The lawmakers called on the Ministry of Defence (MoD) and its suppliers to “work proactively with manufacturers to develop and adopt a suitable faux fur alternative, in line with the Government’s commitment to advancing animal welfare.” The letter said the continued use of real bearskins does not “meet today’s ethical standards” and argued that new orders should be halted while alternative materials are developed. “Most urgently, while this process continues, bears are still being shot with crossbows and killed, their cubs orphaned, and their pelts used to produce new caps,” the lawmakers wrote. Animal rights group People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals (PETA) UK, which has led several campaigns against the use of bearskins, said Freedom of Information data showed that 22 bearskin caps were ordered in 2024 and 96 in 2025. In a 2024 campaign, PETA UK said, “it takes the skin of at least one bear to make a single cap” and claimed that the 526 bearskin hats purchased by the MoD between 2017 and July 2024 represented “at least as many slaughtered bears.” Following the lawmakers’ letter, PETA UK renewed its call for a synthetic alternative, saying in a press release that “the MoD must urgently dedicate its resources to finding a faux fur and end the UK’s support for the slaughter of wildlife overseas.” A defense ministry spokesperson told CNN the MoD “backs replacing bearskin caps with a faux-fur alternative and we have set five tests any alternative must pass.” The spokesperson added that the ministry “would be happy to resume work with PETA on an alternative should they wish to re-engage.” The five requirements from the MoD for any alternatives must cover water absorption, water penetration, appearance, drying rate and compression. A replacement material would also need to be approved by serving guards to ensure it retains its shape during ceremonial duties and is safe and comfortable to wear. A replacement would also need to be assessed for other factors including sustainability, affordability and long-term suitability before being considered as a replacement for real bearskin. The caps The bearskin caps are most commonly associated with the King’s Guard, whose soldiers stand watch outside Buckingham Palace and other royal residences. They are also a prominent feature of state and ceremonial occasions, including the King’s Birthday Parade, also known as Trooping the Colour, and the State Opening of Parliament. The soldiers who make up the King’s Guard are drawn from the British Army’s five Foot Guards regiments: the Grenadier Guards, Coldstream Guards, Scots Guards, Irish Guards and Welsh Guards, all of whom wear the distinct bearskin cap on ceremonial duties. Dating back to the early 19th century, the caps were intended to make soldiers appear taller and more imposing on the battlefield. Built around a wicker frame, the caps stand at about 45 centimetres (18 inches) tall. The Welsh Guards say they are carefully maintained and are “brushed, steamed and even shampooed” to keep the fur clean and in shape. With proper care, a bearskin cap can remain in service for decades. Some caps currently in use are more than 40 years old, according to the Welsh Guards. The UK government said in April that each bearskin cap costs about £2,460 (about $3,300) to procure. Based on Freedom of Information data, PETA UK estimated that the MoD spent more than £1 million ($1.3 million) on bearskin caps between 2017 and 2024.
